subsidize

/SUB-sih-dyze/ - the stress falls on SUB · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Subsidize means to support with money; to pay part of the cost of something.

For a century the crown subsidized the royal glassworks, buying half its coal so the furnaces never went cold.

Example

Day boats were losing the ice war: the big trawlers had freezer holds, and the co-op's icehouse charged what ice costs. So the port council now subsidizes every small boat's ice, paying forty percent of the bill straight from the town's accounts. The fleet did not get richer — it got possible.

Subsidize is the exact word for what the council does, because subsidize means to support with money — to pay part of the cost of something — and the part matters: the boats still buy their ice, just not alone. Donate would be a one-time gift; a subsidy is scheduled money with a policy behind it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

fund: To fund something, said plainly, is to be the money behind it — a funded lab expects every bill covered. Subsidize claims less on purpose: it means paying part of the cost, a share alongside what the farmer, rider, or patient still pays. The part is the point.

underwrite: To underwrite something is to promise in advance to absorb its cost or risk so others can safely proceed — the underwriter stands behind possible losses that may never arrive. Subsidize is steadier and plainer: actually paying part of an ongoing bill, season after season, as standing policy.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

defund: pull the supporting money back out

burden: load something with costs instead of easing them

Where it sits · how much of the cost is covered

chip in → subsidize → bankroll

chip in vs. subsidize: Chipping in is much lighter than subsidizing: a few dollars toward the office gift is chipping in, while subsidizing means steadily paying a real share of something's cost.

bankroll vs. subsidize: Bankroll goes further than subsidize — a subsidized clinic still bills for part of each visit, while a bankrolled one has its every cost carried by someone else.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — sub-: under, behind (Latin)

Root — sid: to sit (Latin sedere)

Suffix — -ize: verb ending: to make happen

Put it together: Sub- (behind) + sid (to sit) + -ize = to be the thing sitting behind. Latin subsidium named the reserve troops seated behind the battle line, ready to prop up the front. A subsidy is still that: support sitting behind someone's effort, taking part of the weight.

Use the root in a new word: reside: A family that resides on Elm Street sits there day after day — the same sedere, settled instead of standing behind.

Word Building

Word Choice

neutral / policy

Subsidize is budget language: governments, councils, and endowments subsidize fares, lunches, and clinics — ongoing, partial, on purpose. Its unit-mates give differently: a benefactor gives as a person, and largess and munificence describe gifts, not line items. If the support recurs and covers part of a price, subsidize is the precise word.
